what: The lane state is a tea machine, but an LLM operator sits on top deciding each next step and waiting for CI. An operator run that only waited for CI and passed the PR to a reviewer cost about 110k-120k tokens.
cause: fabrika's operate skill puts the drive loop in a prompt; the machine only records what the agent reports.
fix: The machine picks the next step itself. Waiting for CI is a Listen (CI reports back on its own), so no agent waits.
test: Sum operator tokens in runs.jsonl against builder and reviewer tokens per lane; run the same lane under tea-fabrika and compare.

what: A builder stopped on a decision ticket because the ruling answered one of three asks. It recorded BLOCKED with no cause. With no cause, the park can only be cleared by a person, so the whole epic waited.
cause: fabrika 0.9.0 has no park cause for 'ruling owed'; a builder's stop is free text plus a token, not a typed answer.
fix: The builder's stop is a typed value with a required cause (e.g. ruling-incomplete, naming the missing asks). A stop with no cause can't be built.
test: Count parks with no cause in runs.jsonl over time; zero once the answer is typed.

what: The ruling posted on a decision ticket answered the bump per tier but not the two other asks in the same criterion (changelog callout per tier, and whether the policy doc gains a sentence). The lane was unblocked on it anyway and a builder found the gap later.
cause: Nothing compares a ruling with the criterion it is meant to settle before the lane moves on.
fix: Before an unblock, check the ruling against each ask in the criterion: code splits the asks, a narrow Judge answers 'does this ruling answer ask N?' per ask. A miss goes back to the person at once, not after a builder spends a run.
test: Replay: decision tickets with rulings; count rulings that would have been sent back.

what: Epic children run in phases. #609 doesn't depend on #612, but #612 is in phase 1, so #609 can't start while #612 is parked. Moving it means re-planning the epic.
cause: The plan is a list of phases, not the real dependency edges.
fix: The parent is written by hand with real edges, so a child starts when its own inputs are ready.
test: Per epic, compare wall time under phases with wall time under the dependency graph.

what: The epic's plan approval went stale after a ruling on one child changed that child's labels, and had to be given again.
cause: Approval is checked against a snapshot of labels, so any later label change reads as a changed plan.
fix: The approval is an event in the epic's own log, bound to the plan's content, not to label snapshots.
test: Count re-approvals per epic.

what: The skills tell the operator to run lane worktree, lane cleanup and lane leave; the installed CLI (0.9.0) has none of them. Every run skipped them, and agent working copies piled up on disk.
cause: Skill text and CLI ship separately and drifted.
fix: Cleanup is an Act in code that ships with the machine, run when the lane ends. No prose step to skip.
test: Count leftover working copies after a day of lanes.

what: A plugin reload dropped every fabrika agent type from the session. Two operators stopped mid-lane because they could no longer spawn a reviewer, and the lanes waited until the plugin loaded again.
cause: The marketplace source in the user settings (a local folder) didn't match the installed marketplace (GitHub), so the plugin was ignored on reload.
fix: Roles are code the machine calls, not agent types loaded from config at run time. A config problem fails at start, not mid-lane.
test: Count lanes stopped by tooling, not by the work.

what: Another PR merged first, so the lane's PR conflicted while in review. The machine had no step for 'base conflicted' in review and refused the report. The operator parked itself, ran a repair builder, and cleared its own park by hand.
cause: fabrika 0.9.0's review state has no arm for a base conflict.
fix: A base change is something the lane listens for; a conflict while in review goes to repair as a normal step.
test: Count conflicts handled by hand in runs.jsonl.

what: build check is red on every lane because of one guard (codeowners-cp) that doesn't apply to this repo. Every builder and every operator brief has to say 'ignore this one'.
cause: The guard reads a CODEOWNERS shape meant for another repo.
fix: A check that is always red teaches agents to ignore red. Checks are per repo, in settings, and one that can't apply is off.
test: Count briefs that carry an 'ignore this red' line.

what: An operator was asked to report before its reviewer finished. It stopped, and the reviewer ended its turn while waiting on CI, so neither was driving and a new operator had to be started to carry on.
cause: A child agent's life is tied to its parent's turn, not to the lane.
fix: The wait belongs to the machine; a child that waits is a Sub the machine owns, so stopping the driver doesn't drop it.
test: Count lanes where a child was left with no parent.

what: The driver merged a ROADMAP PR by hand with gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch on a repo with a merge queue. The merge failed, and --delete-branch closed the PR; it had to be reopened.
cause: A world-changing step was open to the driver instead of only to the shipper.
fix: Merge is an Act only the machine can take, through the queue. The driver has no merge verb.
test: Count merges not made by the shipper.

what: A criterion lists 8 files from a grep for a name; 2 of them mention the name only in comments. The builder noticed the list is wrong, but only a person can fix the ticket.
cause: The criterion's file set was written from text search, not from what the code uses.
fix: Code facts (code-graph) gather where a name is used, and vetting checks every file a criterion names before the ticket is ready.
test: Replay: count criteria whose file sets disagree with code-graph.

what: A gap report was filed and then closed the same day as working as designed: the spec already says abstract methods aren't nodes.
cause: The report was written before reading the spec section it touched.
fix: Before a report is filed, gather the spec and doc pages that name the thing (facts read the doc pages a ticket names), and show the reporter any that already answer it.
test: Count reports closed as by-design.

what: The triager corrected the brief it was given: the brief said #609 builds on the function #616 changes; reading #609 showed it doesn't. It wrote the correction as a note instead of acting on the wrong claim.
cause: The triager read the source instead of trusting the brief.
fix: Keep it: claims in a brief are checked against the source before they shape a ticket.
test: Count brief claims a stage corrected.

what: The reviewer built the base and the head, ran the ticket's exact fixture twice on the head (byte-identical), and compared hashes of the whole package's output on base and head to show nothing else moved.
fix: Make this the default check: run the fixture on head twice and base once, and diff the whole package's output.
test: Replay: does a base/head output diff catch the extra changes found by hand in past reviews?

what: After a ruling, the unblock had to be typed by hand from the main checkout (decision rule, then lane transition). Running the transition twice was refused the second time with an engine error, not a 'already done' answer.
cause: The unblock is a separate hand step and the transition isn't idempotent.
fix: ask = Act + Listen: the lane posts the question and listens for the ruling; when it lands and passes the check (note 03), the lane moves on by itself.
test: Count hand transitions per ruling.

what: Three sibling issues were triaged in parallel and gave three different answers to the same question, where they live. One parked and asked the owner; two put themselves on an existing milestone at p1. The owner then chose a new campaign, so all three had to be moved again, partly by hand.
cause: Each triager judged the home alone; nothing shared one answer across the batch.
fix: A question that several tickets share is asked once for the batch. Every sibling listens for that one answer instead of guessing its own.
test: Count batches where siblings got different homes, then a re-home.

what: Claim markers left by finished triage runs held the issues for about 50 minutes. A re-home triager sat waiting for them and was stopped (the driver moved the milestones by hand). The run that finished #599's triage took 25 minutes, most of it waiting for a sibling claim to expire.
fix: Who holds a lane is lane state, released when the run ends, not a timed marker that outlives it.
test: Sum minutes runs spend waiting on claims in runs.jsonl.

what: Three triagers in parallel each ran npx to get the same code-graph build. One failed on the shared npx cache (ENOTEMPTY) and had to install its own copy.
fix: Code facts are gathered once by code and handed to every run, so parallel agents don't each fetch the same tool.
test: Count runs that fetch a tool another run already fetched.

what: The driver started a shipper without its own working copy. The ship verb refused at once (exit 33) and the shipper read nothing. It also had no review verdicts to ship on. This is the run right before the hand merge in note 11.
cause: The ship verb refuses to run from the main checkout, and the driver's spawn didn't ask for a separate copy.
fix: The machine starts each role with the setup that role needs (its own copy, verdicts in place). The driver can't start a shipper wrong.
test: Count role runs refused for setup, not for the work.

what: The driver started separate operators on two children of an epic. The #612 operator stopped at once: a child can't get a lane while its epic has none (lane open exit 48). The driver stopped the #608 one and started a single operator on the epic.
cause: Epic children only run inside the epic's lane; the driver didn't know that when it spawned them.
fix: The machine decides what runs next from the epic's own state. There is no driver choosing which ticket gets an operator.
test: Count operators stopped because they were started on the wrong ticket.

what: The epic plan says child #609 needs #601, which is not a child of the epic. Starting the epic lane refused on that (exit 16). The operator restarted it with a flag that drops the edge, then checked by hand that the epic branch already held #601's commit.
cause: The lane machine only knows edges between the epic's own children.
fix: The parent is written with real edges, including edges to work outside the epic; the lane listens for that outside ticket to land.
test: Count plan edges dropped or checked by hand.

what: The owner's ruling on decision child #612 was already a comment, but the first builder couldn't see it: claim refused the decision ticket (exit 30) because no ruling had been recorded with a separate command, and the builder had no verb to read the thread. The lane parked with no cause. The operator then recorded the ruling, but the park still needed a person to clear it.
cause: A ruling only counts once a second command stamps it; the comment itself is not an event the lane sees.
fix: The ruling comment is the event. The lane listens on the ticket, so a posted ruling reaches it without a stamping step.
test: Count builder runs spent on decision tickets before their ruling was recorded.

what: Two triagers gave different shapes for the pitch approval line. One said it must carry a UTC timestamp and that an agent must never post it; the other said there is no timestamp and the line is the whole grammar. The approvals were then posted in both shapes.
fix: An approval is a typed event with one schema, checked when it lands, so no agent has to describe the grammar.
test: Count approvals rejected or re-posted for shape.

what: A reviewer's non-blocking note (abstract-method overloads missing from headers) was filed as #615. Its triager built the code and ran a test file: abstract methods aren't nodes at all, by the spec, so there was nothing to fix. The note had come from reading the code, not running it.
cause: The triager found the note was written from reading one function; no fixture backed it.
fix: A review note only becomes a follow-up after a small fixture shows the gap. A note with no run behind it stays a note.
test: Count follow-ups from review notes closed as by-design.

what: Two lanes went from triaged to merged with no person and no repair: one build, one review, one ship each, about 31-34 minutes. Token split per lane: operator 27% and 32%, builder 42% and 34%, reviewer 23% and 24%, shipper 8% and 10% (437k and 373k tokens in all).
fix: The happy path works; the operator's quarter to a third of the spend is the part machine-drives would remove.
test: Run the same kind of lane under tea-fabrika and compare the total against these two.

what: Where lane leave did exist, it still couldn't clean up: it exited 74 because the agent's own working copy is locked by the harness while that agent is running.
cause: The error says the working tree is locked by the running agent.
fix: Cleanup is an Act the machine runs after the agent has ended, not a step the agent runs on itself.
test: Count working copies left after lanes end.

what: Four lanes in the same package ran at once. #599's PR conflicted twice as the others merged first: once in review, once at ship. Each time it went back to a builder, then CI, then a fresh review, before it could land. Both conflicts were in the same spec section, and both were resolved by keeping both sides.
cause: Parallel lanes in one package edit the same shared doc; nothing orders them or merges the doc mechanically.
fix: The lane listens for main moving; a conflict in a doc both sides only append to goes to a cheap code merge or a narrow repair, not a full build-review cycle. Lanes that touch the same spec section are ordered by the parent.
test: Per lane, count rebuild-and-review cycles caused only by a base move.

what: An operator's first turn already holds about 88k tokens, before it reads the lane: the operate skill is 2,556 lines. A run that made 9 tool calls still reported 104k. Most of what an operator costs is being told how to operate.
cause: Read from the operator transcripts: the context size at the first turn of two short runs.
fix: The routing table, the park causes and the recipes are code (src/fabrika.ts). Nothing reads the skill, so that starting cost is gone, not shrunk.
test: Experiment 48: the machine's row in runs.jsonl is 0 tokens; compare a lane's total against #600 and #601.

what: Across the day's 13 operator runs, about 132 next-step choices, counted by hand. About 88 were routing by state name. 44 were not; 20 of those were the agent working around its setup (no CLI in its working copy, verbs the CLI lacks). Of the 24 real judgment calls, a code rule decides 14, one narrow Jev question fits 9, and 1 needed a person.
cause: Counted from the transcripts' commands and the text around the non-routine steps; the totals are rough, the 17 kinds of call are exact.
fix: The 14 are rules in the operator machine or in the Fabrika service's typed answers; the 9 are named Judge questions, not built yet; the 1 is an ask.
test: Experiment 48's step-0 table: rerun the count on a later day and see which rows are gone.

what: 7 of 13 operator runs stopped short of the lane's end. Three were the driver's doing, two lost their agent types to a plugin reload, and two parked for a person. Only one of those two needed a person: the other waited on a ruling that was already recorded, because the park had no cause and the recipe will not clear a park with none.
cause: The park was a bare BLOCKED; recipe unpark refuses one at exit 12.
fix: A park always carries a typed cause. A ruling-owed park clears by a recipe once a ruling newer than the park stands; only a ruling that leaves a question open goes to ask.
test: Count parks that reached a person, and how many of them a person had already answered.

what: One epic operator carried five children from build to landed on the epic branch in one run of about 131 minutes, each with its own review, then assembled one green PR. It stopped once, at the right place: the PR changes a protected workflow file and no owner had approved it. The park has a typed cause, and the shells filed five follow-up issues on the way.
fix: Keep it: a protected path is a gate with a typed cause that only a named person can pass. The machine can know this stop is coming from the plan (one child touches a protected file) and ask for the approval while the other children build, instead of at the end.
test: Per epic, time from last child landed to merged; compare asking at plan time with asking at ship time.

what: A lane ran from claim to merged with no operator agent. tea-fabrika's operator machine claimed it, made one working copy, ran a builder, waited 7 minutes on CI, ran a reviewer and a shipper, posted the record, removed the copy and released the lane, in 18.8 minutes. Its own spend was 22 Cmds and 60 fabrika verbs: no tokens, no Jev call, no person. The three shells cost $1.74.
fix: Keep it. The operator's 116k to 119k tokens on a clean lane are gone; the shells are unchanged.
test: Run it on a code issue that takes a repair round, and on two lanes at once, before calling it a rate.

what: A wiring check claimed a real issue. A builder shell started through the Agent SDK as the main agent had no skill in its context, called the Skill tool, and the build skill (declared to run as a second agent in the background) picked the next ready issue, claimed #593, read it, and released the claim. Nothing was left on the issue.
cause: Checked in the dry run's log: an agent definition's preloaded skills only reach a subagent spawn, not an SDK session's main agent.
fix: The host puts the shell's skill in front of its brief in code, the Check refuses the Skill tool for a skill already loaded, and a dry run gets read-only tools.
test: The preload and runner dry runs: the shell quotes its skill back with no tool call, and ends with a typed last word.

what: The shipper still ran lane cleanup, a verb the installed CLI does not have, got exit 1, and told the person the lane's working copies were left on disk. They were not: the machine removed its one copy four seconds after the lane's record was posted.
cause: The skill is newer than the pinned CLI (0.9.0), and it still owns a cleanup step the machine now does.
fix: Take cleanup out of the shells' skills when a machine drives: the copy is the machine's from make to remove. Until then the shell's closing words about leftover copies are wrong and should not reach a person.
test: git worktree list before and after a lane; count shell closings that mention leftover copies.

what: Two things broke the typed last word before any lane ran. The SDK refused the answer's JSON Schema because of the $schema line zod adds, and the run died before its first turn. With that fixed, a named agent with its own tool list never got the SDK's answer tool, so its answer came back empty.
cause: Both seen in the runner dry run.
fix: The schema is sent without $schema. When the SDK hands back no structured answer, code reads the last JSON object in the shell's closing text that fits the schema; anything else is null, never text.
test: On #559 all three shells' last words parsed: SHIPPED-PR, PASS, LANDED. None was needed, because each shell's own report landed.

what: Where the 18.8 minutes went: 11.1 in the three shells, 7 waiting for CI before review, under 1 in the machine. The shipper's 6.5 minutes were almost all its own wait on checks and the merge queue, with an opus session held open and idle.
cause: Read from the run's log: the times of each Cmd, each shell's start and end.
fix: The wait before review is already a Listen and cost nothing. The shipper's waits could be Listens too: a Check for its gates, an Act to enqueue, a Listen on the queue, and no agent.
test: Ship one lane with the gates as code and compare the 6.5 minutes and $0.30.

what: Five sibling issues were triaged in parallel, each told its home up front (milestone 7). All five agreed, and none waited on another: 2.1 to 3.1 minutes and 72k to 81k tokens each. The morning before, three siblings given no home gave three different answers (note 2026-10-10-17).
cause: The one fact that differed between the two batches was the home, handed in with the task instead of left for each triager to work out.
fix: Keep it. A fact siblings share is gathered once, before they start, and handed to each as data. Nothing a parallel agent has to guess should be something its parent already knows.
test: Per triage batch, count siblings whose home differs from the batch's and how many had to be moved after.

what: A lane failed its first review and was repaired with no operator agent and no person. The first PR's required check went red on CI (a second stderr line that only shows on Linux). The machine saw the checks settle, started the reviewer, the reviewer read the failing log and failed both verdicts, the lane went back to build, a builder found and fixed the cause, the second review passed, and the PR merged through the queue. 40.2 minutes, $7.68, 49 Cmds, no tokens of the machine's own.
fix: Keep it. The repair loop needed no new code: review's FAIL folds the lane back to build, and the routing table sends build to a builder whatever round it is.
test: Run more lanes that fail review; this is one.

what: Three builders in a row were recorded dead though each had finished its work. Each pushed or checked the repair, started its wait on CI as a background command, and ended its turn to wait. Under the machine a shell is the one agent of a one-shot session, so the session ended there, with no report to the lane. The machine recorded a dead shell and started the next builder, which did the same, until CI finished and the fifth one could report. The three extra builders cost $1.94, a quarter of the lane.
cause: Read in the shells' transcripts: run_in_background true on the CI wait, then the turn ends. A Claude Code subagent is woken when a background command finishes; an SDK session's main agent is not.
fix: Now: the Check refuses a background command and the shell is told why. Better: the builder should not wait on CI at all. The machine already listens to the PR's checks before review, for free. And a shell that ends with no report should be asked to finish in its own conversation, not replaced by a new one that reads everything again.
test: Count dead-shell laps per lane, and how many of those shells had pushed work.

what: The Check before each shell step refused two harmless commands: one redirecting to /dev/null inside a subshell, one to /dev/stdout. It read both as writes outside the working copy. The builder reworded each and went on.
cause: The path rule took a closing bracket as part of the path, and knew /dev/null but no other device.
fix: Fixed: a path loses what closes a subshell, and anything under /dev is no file. A Check that refuses what is fine teaches a shell to route around it, which is the opposite of its job.
test: Per lane, count refusals and how many were right. On #625: 2 refusals, 0 right.

what: The first reviewer was started on a PR whose required check was already red. It spent $1.00 and 2.2 minutes, and its finding was the CI failure, read from the log, with a likely cause. The machine knew the checks were red before it started the reviewer.
cause: The machine waits for checks to settle, green or red, then briefs the reviewer either way.
fix: Not decided. A gate could send a red PR straight back to the builder with the failing job's log, and skip the reviewer. But this reviewer's note (the fix belongs in the product, not in a looser test) is the kind of steer a log does not carry.
test: On lanes whose first review fails on red CI, compare the repair with and without the reviewer's note.

what: Before a review, four operator runs read the PR's checks as still running. Three started the reviewer anyway (the tail PR of #604, #605, and #616, where the merge state was also unknown after three reads). One waited (#599). The skill says wait. Given the same tool output, Jev and Opus both answered wait all four times.
cause: Read in the operator transcripts: the build verdicts output and the command after it. Nothing in the lane stops a reviewer from starting on checks that have not settled, so it is left to each operator.
fix: Already in the machine: the review turn listens until the checks settle, as a rule in code. No Judge is needed for it, and agreeing with a rule is no reason to pay for a call.
test: experiment 51, the gate cases: Jev matched Opus on the same text 7 of 7 and matched the operators 2 of 5.
